items.title: For investors with long horizons and focus on underlying businesses: 5 mid- and small-cap stocks with upside potential of up to 34%
items.description: Here’s one thing to remember: Be very careful when you use fresh money to average down a stock because it has fallen. Averaging is not a strategy if the original investment thesis has weakened. In many cases, the habit of averaging only increases the size of the eventual loss. Fresh capital deserves fresh ideas.

items.title: F&O Talk: 25,500 remains crucial support for Nifty, says Sudeep Shah; gives RIL, HDFC Bank strategy
items.description: The Sensex and Nifty extended their rally as a stronger rupee, record foreign inflows and gains in banking stocks boosted sentiment. Analysts expect the bullish trend to continue but see possible near-term consolidation as technical indicators approach overbought levels.

items.title: 5 penny stocks plunge up to 68% in six months. Do you own any?
items.description: Over the past six months, five penny stocks from the BSE Smallcap index have corrected sharply, falling between 21% and 68%. These stocks were identified through a screen of companies with a market capitalisation of less than Rs 1,000 crore, a share price below Rs 20 and a minimum recent trading volume of 5 lakh shares. The screen captures low-priced, relatively liquid penny stocks that have witnessed significant price declines during the period. (Data Source: ACE Equity).

items.title: Nifty scales nine-month high, 26K in sight: 5 triggers that could drive or derail D-Street rally this week
items.description: Indian equities rose for a fourth straight week, with the Nifty and Sensex reaching nine-month highs. FII flows, inflation, crude oil, the rupee and global cues will shape the Nifty’s push toward 26,000.

items.title: Tyres stocks: A contrarian, tactical bet in the current market? 4 stocks with upside potential of up to 19%, according to analysts
items.description: The problem that has hit tyre companies in recent times was not lack of demand. It was the cost of their crude-linked raw materials, and that cost is now easing as oil prices come down. Demand had held up throughout, so the squeeze that hurt them is now reversing. Is the worst behind the tyre business?
